html:
Galata was the walled Genoese town across the Golden Horn from Constantinople, from 1267 until the Ottoman conquest in 1453. From there Genoa controlled much of the trade of the Black Sea.

In 1261 Michael VIII Palaiologos gave Genoa wide trading rights in the Treaty of Nymphaeum, to win its help against Venice and the Latins. After first lodging the Genoese in the city, he moved them to Galata in 1267, where they could be watched. The colony, also called Pera, soon had its own walls, its own governor and its own laws.

Its merchants carried grain, salt fish, furs and slaves from Genoese ports in Crimea such as Caffa, and its customs income came to exceed that of the Byzantine capital itself. In 1348 the Genoese built the Galata Tower and fought the Byzantine navy. In 1453 Galata stayed neutral, and it surrendered to Mehmed II after the city fell. It became a district of Ottoman Istanbul, home to foreign merchants and envoys, and is now Karaköy.
sum: Galata was the walled Genoese town across the Golden Horn from Constantinople, from 1267 until the Ottoman conquest in 1453. From there Genoa controlled much of the trade of the Black Sea.
